la:noun:ovum.html:
ōvum, i, n.
ὠόν, i. e. ΩϝΟΝ
.
Lit., an egg: ovum parere,to lay,; : edere,: ponere,: efferre,: eniti,: facere,: pullos ex ovis excuderunt,to hatch, B. and K. (al. excluserunt): incubare ova,to sit on, brood on, hatch,; ; for which: incubare ovis,: suppovere ova,: an pulli rostellis ova percuderint ... nam saepe propter crassitudinem putaminum erumpere non queunt,: quatenus in pullos animalis vertier ova cernimus alituum,.—Also of the spawn of fish, etc.: etsi pisces, ova cum genuerunt relinquunt,: testudines autem et crocodilos dicunt ... obruere ova,: saepius et tectis penetralibus extulit ova ... formica,; : ovi putamen,an eggshell,: cortex ovi,.—The Romans usually began their meals with eggs and ended them with fruit; hence, integram famem ad ovum affero, until the egg, i. e. the beginning of the meal, ; and: ab ovo Usque ad mala citaret, Io Bacche!i. e. from the beginning to the end,.—Acc. to the myth, Leda became pregnant by Jupiter, who visited her in the shape of a swan; she laid two eggs, one by Jupiter, and the other by Tyndarus; from the former of which were born Pollux and Helen, and from the latter Castor and Clytaemnestra; hence, nec gemino bellum Trojanum orditur ab ovo,: Castor gaudet equis, ovo prognatus eodem Pugnis, from the same egg, i. e. of the same parentage, .—In the circus seven wooden eggs were set up, one of which was removed at the completion of each circuit; hence, non modo ovum illud sublatum est, quod, etc.,: ova ad notas curriculis numerandis,.—
Transf.
An egg-shell (as a measure), an egg-shellful, .—
An egg-shape, oval shape, oval, .

la:noun:ovis.html:
ŏvis, is (acc. ovim, ; al. ovem; abl. ovi, acc. to Müll.), f. (m., Varr. ap. :
ovis mas,; cf.: ovis semimas,; cf. Müll.) [kindr. with Sanscr. avi, ovis; Lith. awi-s; Slav. ovjza; Gr. ὄϊς; cf. also Goth. avistr, ovile], a sheep (class.).
Lit.: oves scabrae, glabrae,: cum fervit maxime, tam placidum quasi ovem reddo,; : multae dictione ovium et boum,: ovis bona,: aurata,: infirmae,: lanigera,: Milesiae,: nigra,: pinguis,: placida,: custos ovium,: magistri ovium,: tondere oves,.— Prov.: ovem lupo committere,to appoint the wolf shepherd,; cf.: O praeclarum custodem ovium, ut ajunt, lupum,.—
Transf.
Poet., wool: et niveam Tyrio murice tingit ovem,.—
Sheep, for simpleton, ninny, fool, , q. v. 15.

senses: to applaud, celebrate with an ovation
la:verb:ovo.html:
ŏvo, ātum (
first pers. pres. indic. and perf. forms not in use: ovet,: ovaret,: ovandi,; : ovaturus,), 1, v. defect. n. [cf. Sanscr. root u-, avate, to roar; Gr. αὔω, ἀϝυω, to shout], to exult, rejoice.
In gen. (mostly poet.): ovantes Horatium accipiunt,: laetus ovat nunc laude virum,.—Of inanim. subjects: currus ovantes, (4, 8), 53: ovat Africus,rages,.—
In partic., to celebrate or keep an ovation, to triumph in an ovation (v. ovatio; freq. and class.): ovantem in Capitolium ascendere,: ovans urbem ingrederetur,: ovans triumphavit,made his triumphal entry on foot,; : ovatum aurum,brought in in triumph, taken as spoil,. —Hence, P. a.: ŏvans, antis, exulting, joyful, triumphant: socii comitentur ovantes,; cf.: ovantes gutture corvi,i. e. singing, uttering exultant cries,; ; .—Transf., of things: prosequar et currus utroque ab litore ovantes, (4, 8), 53: lyra,: patria,.—Hence,

ŏvanter, adv., exultingly (post-class.): ovanter accurrit,.
